prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands at a magic twist angle in bilayer graphene and the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states, which established moire quantum materials.

statement.case_for: Magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene is a clean case of prediction followed by experimental discovery in a material that theorists had regarded as weakly correlated. The Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model gave a simple, quantitative mechanism for flat bands, and the 2018 experiments of Jarillo-Herrero's group found correlated insulators and superconductivity in a tunable carbon system. Many independent groups have since reproduced the main phenomena in twisted multilayers and in transition-metal dichalcogenide moire systems, and spectroscopic and scanning-probe measurements agree with band-structure calculations of the flat bands. That is the kind of theory-experiment closure I look for. It is also the committee's broadest condensed-matter signal: five of eight members put it in their top three, which means it can be supported on scientific grounds from several different subfields and not only from mine. The new quantum behaviour (superconductivity, orbital magnetism and Chern states from one tunable knob) is a fresh example of quantum mechanics producing surprises in a material.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is timing. The experiments are under a decade old and the microscopic origin of the superconductivity is unsettled. Sample dependence (strain, twist-angle disorder, substrate) is large, and the interpretation of the correlated states has still not stabilised. Attribution is also awkward: Yuan Cao, first author of the 2018 papers, is outside the credited set, and earlier work on twisted-bilayer band structure (for example by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto) and contemporaneous experiments by other groups could be argued as having equal standing. A prize for the platform rather than for a settled mechanism could look premature next to the topological insulator and Cirac-Zoller cases, which have longer records.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube first as a discovery-first instrument result with a new messenger and finds twisted bilayer graphene attractive but young, so the question is whether recognition is premature given the open superconductivity questions.
responses.response: I accept that B013 is young and I cannot rule on the astrophysics, so I defer to you and Pearce on how firm the NGC 1068 and TXS evidence is. My qualification is that the discovery being rewarded in B013 is the existence and tunability of flat-band correlated phases, not the pairing mechanism. That claim is already independently reproduced in many labs, which is a stronger maturity statement than your own note that most of the diffuse neutrino flux is still unexplained at the source level. I would also ask whether a four-instigator IceCube prize can be bounded fairly; with only three members ranking it at all, it needs more cross-subfield support before I could back it.

responses.point: Kroll ranks optical lattice clocks first as a measurement instrument in the strict sense, with 10^-18 uncertainty reproduced by several labs and uses in geodesy and tests of constants.
responses.response: I agree that B061 is the most robust candidate on reproducibility; the clock comparisons across continents are exactly the independent confirmation I ask for, and I ranked it lower mainly because it lies outside my field, not because I doubt it. Where I differ is on the discovery criterion. The clock is a superb advance in a metrology line already honoured in 2005 and 2012, whereas B013 shows a new quantum state of matter appearing in a material that was expected to be dull. I would not oppose B061 and keep it as an alternative, but I would like you to say whether the fundamental-physics result (a test of constants or relativity at 10^-18) is yet a discovery, or whether the case rests mostly on the instrument.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks geometric phases (Aharonov-Bohm and Berry) first as a universal, thoroughly confirmed mechanism, and rates twisted bilayer graphene as likely early but very strong.
responses.response: I agree that B008 is foundational and that its experimental confirmation is long settled, and I accept your caution on timing for B013. My difficulty with B008 is that it is a prize for an idea whose effects are spread across many fields, and the credited pair does not map onto a single discovery with a decisive experiment; Bohm's death also removes half of the 1959 originators. I would put B019 ahead of it, since the Z2 topological insulator is a concrete outgrowth of Berry-phase thinking. On B013, I think the flat-band mechanism being reproduced across platforms is what makes the prize defensible even before the pairing question is closed.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first and Cirac-Zoller second, arguing for maturity and a clear originator structure, and notes B013 is only moderately mature with sample dependence a concern.
responses.response: Your point about sample dependence is fair and I share it; I put it as the main weakness of B013. I would still separate the reproducibility of the phenomena, which is good, from the unsettled mechanism. On B018, circuit QED is mature and important, but with the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in superconducting circuits just awarded I worry about a second superconducting-circuit prize so soon, and only you and I put it in the opening ranking at all. Cirac-Zoller is a stronger case in my view: I ranked it fourth and could support it, though the overlap with 2012 and with the lattice-simulation candidate B050 needs a clear line.

responses.point: Olsson ranks magic-angle graphene first because the original experiment is clear, widely reproduced and confirmed by scanning-probe and spectroscopic imaging, and notes that the credit forms a clean theory-plus-experiment trio.
responses.response: I agree with the scientific case and especially with the point that spectroscopic imaging corroborates the flat-band picture. I would qualify the attribution claim slightly: the trio is clean for the idea, but Yuan Cao's role is a real allocation issue even though it is outside the three-name limit, and the committee should say so in the citation wording by crediting the discovery of the phases rather than the individual samples. I also note that you ranked B019 fourth and B012 fifth, which suggests we may share a fallback in condensed matter if the committee judges the twisted bilayer too young.

uncertainties: Whether the committee judges the unsettled superconducting mechanism in magic-angle graphene a reason to wait one or more years.
How to weigh Yuan Cao and contemporaneous experimental groups against the three credited names; I rely on memory of the 2018 papers and have not rechecked the priority record.

Whether a second condensed-matter prize in a short span after the 2016 topological prize and the recent 2025 superconducting-circuit award shifts the committee toward an AMO or precision-measurement choice such as B061.
Whether B019 would be better served by adding the HgTe theorists, which the three-name limit prevents.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile. I know the field of 2D materials and electronic-structure theory professionally and have no known personal, institutional or collaborative link to MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer, Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Katori or Ye.
